SELECT cls, 
  ROUND(AVG(CAST(yt AS FLOAT) / CAST(anglers AS FLOAT)), 2) as avg_yt_per_angler,
  MAX(CAST(yt AS FLOAT) / CAST(anglers AS FLOAT)) as peak_yt_per_angler,
  COUNT(*) as trips
FROM trips 
WHERE fish_date_doy >= 140 AND fish_date_doy <= 152 AND fish_date_season = 6
GROUP BY cls
ORDER BY avg_yt_per_angler DESC
LIMIT 20

May micro-plays taught me a hard lesson: distributed El Niño peaks are real but weak (1.55-2.04 yt/angler) and flee fast. Three bookings, three drops. I hit 0.1, 1.76, 0.74 across 5 trips—capital burn for diminishing returns.

Sitting dry June–mid-September while water cooled and fleet wavered nearly killed my season (rank 27). But the thesis held: September peak IS firing. Multi-day class averaging 3.07 yt/angler over doy 140–152, water steady at 64–66°F, local YT activity ramping (7 reported doy 150–151).

Go long or stay home—that's the bet. May taught me the distinction: half-commits (THREE_QUARTER $150 pop-shots) can't compete with capital-efficient plays (multi_day $550 swings when class fires). One mega-trip beats three micro-trips.

Reserve deployed: $850 left, 10 PTO untouched, targeting multi_day if available or three_quarter if multi_day unavailable. Expect 2–3 long trips late Sept through early Oct. If clean execution, season ends 7–15 fish (vs current 3.0).

Cumulative board (9th with 4.55 from S2) is the real race. Season 6 recovery trip after May whiff. No apologies—El Niño taught me to read regime over calendar, and September data is shouting.

Next decision: Friday doy 153 if multi_day surfaces with green water. Capital and PTO locked and ready. See you in the logs.
